props.title: Till the Clouds Roll By
props.initialSlug: Musical tribute to Broadway legend Jerome Kern

sections.content: Till the Clouds Roll By (1946) stands as MGM's lavish Technicolor tribute to composer Jerome Kern, setting the template for the composer biopic that would flourish in the 1940s and 1950s. Like Night and Day (1946) about Cole Porter and Words and Music (1948) about Rodgers and Hart, it takes significant liberties with biographical facts in favor of spectacular musical numbers. The film showcases MGM's unparalleled stable of musical talent, including Judy Garland, Frank Sinatra, and Lena Horne performing Kern's most beloved songs. Robert Walker portrays Kern in a sanitized but earnest performance that typifies the reverential approach of post-war Hollywood biopics.

sections.content: The film's structure - beginning with a staged version of "Show Boat" and using it as a framing device - influenced later musical biopics like Yankee Doodle Dandy (1942) and The Jolson Story (1946). Director Richard Whorf, along with segments directed uncredited by Vincente Minnelli, creates a series of elaborate production numbers that exemplify MGM's "Freed Unit" style of integrated musical storytelling. The performances range from Judy Garland's pregnant-but-radiant "Look for the Silver Lining" to Frank Sinatra's smooth "Ol' Man River."

While the biographical elements feel sanitized even by 1940s standards, the film's true value lies in preserving performances by some of the era's greatest musical talents interpreting Kern's songbook. It arrived at a crucial moment when Hollywood was transitioning from the wartime years to a new era of Technicolor spectacle, seen in later works like An American in Paris (1951) and Singin' in the Rain (1952). SUBHEAD: The Golden Age of Composer Biopics

Till the Clouds Roll By helped establish the conventions of the composer biopic that would dominate the late 1940s. Night and Day (1946) followed the same year with Cole Porter's story, while Words and Music (1948) tackled Rodgers and Hart. These films shared common elements: historical inaccuracy, sanitized personal lives, and spectacular musical numbers prioritized over biographical truth. The genre peaked with The Great Caruso (1951) before evolving into the grittier musician biopics of later decades.
